about: THE SEA'S WORDS (the cards of Data/encounters/sea_793.json): a draft for the user to overwrite. For each card: <id>.title, <id>.fact (the intention line), <id>.say.<name> (a line of speech), <id>.<option> (the option's label, ending in its odds as a word), <id>.<option>.done (what came of it), or <id>.<option>.success and <id>.<option>.failure where the option has a chance, and art.<id> (one line for the artist: who, where, doing what, the hour and the weather). The outcome keys are not read by the panel yet. Plain wording, no mock-archaic; dates by feasts; nobody says adventure.

entries.text: The wind drops
The wind has dropped to nothing, so the sail hangs from the yard like washing and the sea lies as flat as poured lead.
A calm ends when it likes, and a man waits for the wind the way he waits for a ferryman, with no say in when it comes.
We've six oars, four men and a heavy boat, so it'll be a long pull.
Out oars and row
Four oars do not move a laden boat far, and by evening the men's hands are raw and the shore has moved by the width of a finger.
Lie quiet and wait for it
Toward evening the water darkens to the west, the sail lifts, and she begins to talk under the bow again.
The calm holds all through the night, and nobody sleeps well on a boat that does not move.
Put lines over the side while she lies
The lines bring up whiting and one fat cod, and fresh fish on a calm evening is as good as the sea ever gets.
Nothing bites, and the lines hang as straight and as still as the sail.
The boat on a flat grey sea at noon, the square sail hanging slack, four men sitting idle and one trailing a hand in the water; haze, no horizon.
A calm night
There is no wind and hardly any moon, and the boat lies so still that the men can hear each other breathe. None of them is sleepy.
Somebody tell us something, as long as it is not the one about the reeve's wife again.
My people have sayings for a night like this. Short ones, mind, so you'll not have to stay awake long.
Let Ravn say his people's sayings

He says them flatly, like a man counting his stock. Praise the day when it is evening, he says, and the ice when you have crossed it, and the ale when you have drunk it. The steersman says it is the first sensible thing he has ever heard from a heathen.
Read the swimming match of Beowulf and Breca from your chest

Beowulf swims five nights in the sea in a mail coat, with a sword in one hand to keep off the whales. The lookout wants to know how he ate, and since nobody has an answer, the argument lasts until the wind comes.
Tell the one about the island that sank
Some sailors moor to an island and light a fire for their supper, and the island dives to cool its back, because it was a whale all along. The men laugh in the dark.
You tell it too well, and the youngest hand lies awake until dawn watching the water for islands.
Night on a flat black sea, seen from the bow: five shapes lying among the cargo under the furled sail, one sitting up with a hand raised, talking; a few stars, no moon.
Becalmed beside a stranger

Another ship lies in the same calm a long bowshot away, clinker-built with one square sail hanging slack, and she belongs to Northmen by the cut of her. There is nowhere worth rowing to for either of you, and her master is holding up a horn cup.
There is no wind for you and none for me, so there is no quarrel between us either. Come over and drink, and I will ask you something that my grandfather once asked me.
He's asking you over to drink, and a man who wanted your cargo wouldn't ask first.
Row across and drink with him

His ale is thin, but his question is a good one. He asks what it was that he drank yesterday, which was neither wine nor water, neither mead nor beer, and still left him with no thirst. He will not tell you the answer, and says only that you will meet it yourself some morning.
Buy a bundle of his whetstones, for six pennies' weight of silver
You get a bundle of grey whetstones from the north, each of which he tries on a knife first. He weighs your pennies on a folding scale as if they were scrap silver, and keeps them.
Keep your distance and your oars ready
He shrugs, drinks the cup himself, and sits down. The two ships lie and look at each other until the wind comes.
Two small ships lying still on a glassy sea in summer daylight, sails slack; on the nearer one a bearded Northman stands at the gunwale holding up a drinking horn toward the viewer.
Five names for a calm

A ship of the Northmen lies in the same calm, close enough to count her oar-ports. Her master is sitting on the gunwale with his feet over the side, and he seems to have been waiting for someone to talk to.
Men call this a calm, but I know five other names for it from five other kinds of folk, and not one of those names makes it blow. Do you know them?
It's a game from the halls, what each kind of being calls a thing. He'll give you the names and keep the answer.
Hear his names for the calm

He says that the gods call it the Quiet, the giants call it the Sultry, and the dwarfs call it the Shelter of Day. He leaves it to you to say what the thing itself is, although it is lying all round you.
Buy one of his soapstone pots, for five pennies' weight of silver

You get a soapstone pot from the north, of the kind that sits in the fire for a lifetime and never cracks. He weighs your silver, and throws in some advice about the wind that is of no use to anybody today.
Keep your distance and your oars ready
He says the names anyway, to the sea, and since it is a long afternoon you hear most of them twice.
A calm bright sea; a lean Norse ship close alongside, her master sitting on the gunwale with his bare feet hanging over the water, one hand lifted and counting on his fingers.
A long swell
A long, slow swell has begun to lift the boat, and it comes from a quarter the wind is not blowing from. The sky that way is the colour of the inside of a mussel shell.
That swell was made by a wind we have not met yet, and it will be here to introduce itself by evening.
The gulls have all gone in toward the land, every one of them.
The ships that robbed Jarrow went to pieces off the Tyne in weather that began like this, the summer after Lindisfarne, because the sea does not ask a man his faith first.
Shorten sail now and stow for weather
The sail is tied up along its foot to half its height, and everything loose is wedged or lashed down. She goes slower and drier after that, and the men stop looking at the sky.
Turn for the nearest lee and get behind it
You give up half a day's distance and put her head toward the land, and nobody aboard argues with you.
Hold on under full sail while the wind serves
She runs like a horse let out of a yard. You make a full day's distance before dusk, and the swell is still only a swell.
A gust lays her over until the lee gunwale goes under and the sea comes in green. She comes back up again, but a seam in the sail has started to open.

The boat climbing the smooth back of a long grey swell under a pale shell-coloured sky, late afternoon; the steersman looking back over his shoulder to windward, gulls flying away toward a far low shore.
The gale
The gale is here. The wind is taking the tops off the seas and the spray comes aboard flat and hard, and everything that was not lashed down is moving.
She is snug enough, so now it is only a matter of not doing anything clever.
There is too much sail on her and no gentle way to take it off, so tell me what you want and tell me fast.
I've been in worse than this, and I didn't enjoy that either.
Strike the sail and hold her head to it under oars

The yard comes down in a fight of wet wool and rope. Two men at the oars hold her head up to the seas and the others bail by turns until it has blown itself out. Nothing is lost but the day and the skin of their hands.
Run before it under the shortened sail, as you made ready
Under a scrap of sail she runs before it, fast and nearly dry, and the steersman never once takes his eyes off the sea astern. By dusk you are farther along than a fair wind would have put you.
Carry full sail and run for it
She flies before it, and twice she buries her bow and twice she shakes it clear again. When the wind eases you are a day ahead, and nobody aboard can feel their hands.

A sea climbs over the stern and fills her to the thwarts, and the men bail with the bailer, the cooking pot and their hands. She lives through it, but whatever was lowest in the hold is soaked through, and the sail has begun to tear.

The boat small in a steep grey sea, spray blown flat off the crests, the sail a scrap near the foot of the mast; one man braced at the steering oar, the others bent low and bailing; dark sky, daylight failing.
A black line
A hard black line of cloud is coming up against the wind, with a bright edge under it and the sea gone white beneath.
That is a squall, and when it hits us it will turn the wind inside out. It will be short, but it will be nasty.
It is raining under that cloud, and I can see the rain walking across the water.
Drop the sail and take it bare
The yard is down and lashed when it hits. The boat staggers, the rain comes like thrown gravel, and in the time it takes to say the Creed it has gone by.
Drop the sail and spread it to catch the rain
The sail is spread across the thwarts like a trough. When the squall has passed there is a hand's depth of sweet water in it, tasting of wool, and every cask is topped up.
Keep the sail and ride the front of it
For as long as it lasts she goes faster than anyone aboard has ever seen her go, with the steersman's knuckles white on the oar. Then it is past, and you have stolen a piece of the day from it.
The wind comes from the other side all at once and throws the sail back against the mast. She goes over to the gunwale and comes up again, but a seam in the sail has gone.

A summer sea still in sunlight in the foreground, the boat with her yard half lowered; behind her a wall of blue-black cloud with a hard bright lower edge and a white line of broken water under it, rain hanging in grey curtains.
A grey bank
The edge of the sea has gone soft. To windward a low grey bank lies on the water, and it is nearer than it was.
Take a hard look at the land now, because in a little while it will be gone.
I can still see the land, but I shall not see it for much longer.
Take your marks now: fix the land, the sun and the wind in your head
The steersman points and you say it back to him: the church on the dune there, the sun over the left shoulder, the wind on the right cheek. Then the land goes out like a blown lamp.
Close the shore and anchor before it shuts
You find four fathoms over sand and let the anchor go while there is still a shore to see. The fog arrives and finds you already sitting still.
Sail on and trust it to lift
The bank comes down on you between one breath and the next. It is cold inside it, and it smells of wet wool.

A calm silver-grey morning; the boat in clear air in the foreground, the steersman pointing at a low dune with a small church on it, and beyond the bow a wall of pale fog lying on the water and swallowing the far shore.
Blind
The fog is down, and from the stern the stem is only a shadow. Water drips off the yard, and every sound seems to come from every side at once.
We took our marks, so I know where the land was, and I will tell you where it is as soon as I can hear it.
Nobody looked before it shut down on us, so now we either guess or we stop.
Stop her: lie still, sound the horn, and wait
You lie there blind and listening, while a man blows the horn every so often and nothing answers. When the fog lifts, half a day is gone and nothing else is lost.
Feel in for the land by the marks you took

The steersman steers by the wind on his cheek and the count of his own breathing. When the lookout calls sand under the bow, it is the very beach he said it would be, and he does not need to say anything about it.
Creep on under oars with a man sounding in the bow
You go a boat's length at a time, with the pole going down in the bow and the depth called back in a whisper, until you come out of the far side of the fog into plain grey daylight.
The pole finds nothing again and again, and then the keel finds the bottom instead. She grinds over a hard bar and floats again, but now there is water in her where there was none before.

Thick white fog: only the after half of the boat can be seen, the mast fading upward into nothing; a man in the bow is a grey shape leaning over a sounding pole, another holds a cow horn to his mouth.
A horn in the fog
A horn sounds in the fog, low and close, and then it sounds again. It is another ship, feeling her way along as blind as you are.
I think that is a horn and not a cow, though I would not swear to it.
A man who blows a horn in fog is honest, or wants to be taken for it.
Answer with your own horn

A hull slides past close enough to touch, grey in the grey fog, with Northmen aboard and a cargo of hides and whetstones. Her master leans out and shouts something as he goes by, and Ravn says it was a riddle. Who is the huge one that swallows water and woods, fears the wind but no man, and makes war on the sun?
The horn stops, and then you hear oars, a good many of them, coming toward the place you answered from. You pull away hard and blind until the men's arms shake, and nothing finds you.
Keep silent and let her pass
The horn sounds twice more, each time from farther off, and you never learn who she was.
Shout your name, your port and your lading into the fog

A voice shouts back in bad Frisian that they are out of Ripa for the Rhine and have been three days in this soup, and asks where in the name of all the gods the land is. You tell him, and he thanks you and is gone.
Nothing answers you. You have told the fog who you are and what you carry, and the steersman looks at you for some time afterwards.

Dense fog over a still sea; the bow of the boat in the foreground with the lookout crouched and listening, a hand cupped to his ear; ahead, the bare dark outline of another ship's stem coming out of the white.
A sound under the wind
Under the wind there is another sound, a slow and regular fall like a hall door closing a long way off, and it is surf.
Surf on sand makes that sound, and surf on rock is sharper, but either way it is the place where the sea stops.
It is ahead of us... no, it is on the steering side, or at least I think so, because it is hard to say.
Turn away from it and stand off until you can see
You put the sound behind you and keep it there. At first light the shore is just where your ears said it was, a long white line with nothing else to be seen.
Sound your way in toward it and anchor in its lee
The lead finds six fathoms, then four, then three, and then sand. The anchor goes down a bowshot outside the breakers, and the men sleep as they have not slept since port.
The bottom comes up faster than the count, and she strikes once, hard, on the back of a swell before she comes off again. Before morning somebody finds the plank lap that is weeping.
Night or thick mist; the boat seen from astern with all the men turned the same way, listening; far ahead, barely visible, a faint pale line of breaking water.
A ring round the light
A wide pale ring has formed round the light in the sky, a full hand-span out and unbroken all the way round. Inside it the sky is a little darker than outside.
Look at the sun, it has a wheel all the way round it!
Look at the moon, it is wearing a ring!
That is high cloud, as thin as breath on a blade, and it means rain inside a day with wind behind the rain. I have seen it fail, but not often.
Your priests would call that a sign, and so would ours. It's the one thing they agree on.
The English wrote one down in their book of years, a ring round the sun in the summer when a cross stood in the moon. I asked a York man what came of it, and he said that rain came of it.
Read it as weather: lash everything and look for a lee by tomorrow
The cargo is wedged and tied before there is any need. The steersman says nothing, which from him is praise.
Read it as a sign: a prayer now, and a penny vowed to the next altar
The men say the prayer they all know, while Ravn stands politely to one side, and a penny is promised to whichever altar comes first. The ring stays where it is.
Say it is only a ring
You say so, but the men look at it anyway, every time they think you are not watching them.
A thin white sky with a pale sun and a complete wide halo round it; below, small, the boat under sail on a quiet sea with three men looking up, one shading his eyes.
Frost at sea
Dawn comes up red over a flat grey sea. Every rope is furred white, the sail is as stiff as a board, and there is ice in the men's beards.
This is frost at sea, when the ropes will not run and the sail will crack before it bends. Nothing gets hoisted until it has been beaten soft.
In my country they call this autumn.
I cannot feel my feet, and I would like it remembered that I said so.
Beat the ice out of the sail and ropes before you hoist
The men work along the yard with oar-looms and the flat of their hands until the wool bends again, with their breath hanging round them. By the time the sun is clear of the sea she is sailing.
Put them on the oars to get warm
A man at an oar is a warm man. They pull until the steam comes off them and the frost is only on the gunwales.
Hoist as she is: the wind will thaw her
The sail goes up creaking like a door and shakes itself loose in the first puff of wind, with no harm done.
The frozen sail will not bend round the yard. Something in it gives with a small dry sound, and when it thaws there is a seam open.

A red winter sunrise over a flat calm sea; the boat white with rime on rope, yard and gunwale, the sail hanging stiff; men with frosted beards beating at the sail with the handles of their oars, breath smoking.
The bar on the ebb
Ahead, the river meets the sea across its bar. The tide is running out against the wind, and over the bar the water stands up in short steep heaps that break where they stand.
That is the wind blowing against the ebb on a bar. At the turn of the tide it is a ditch you could wade across, but just now it is a row of walls.
There is white water right across it, with no gap that I can see from here.
Anchor and wait for the flood to cover it
You lie to the anchor and watch the breakers shrink as the tide makes. When there is a smooth road over the bar you take it, and it is nothing at all.
Take the cut the fisherman showed you
A boat's length north of where anyone would try, exactly as he said, there is a tongue of dark water with no white on it. You go through with breakers on both hands and a dry boat.
Take it now, bows on, with the men at the oars
She climbs the first one, falls off the back of it, and climbs the next. Then it is behind you, and the men are laughing the way men laugh when they have been frightened.

The third sea breaks aboard, and for a moment she is a trough full of water with oars sticking out of it. She strikes the sand twice and drives over. You bail until the turn of the tide, and a plank is weeping.

A low sandy river mouth under a windy sky; a line of short white breakers right across the channel, brown ebb water pouring out through them; the boat held off under oars in the foreground, the lookout standing in the bow.
The look of the water
The water ahead has changed colour from green to brown, with a slick, smooth patch where the sea ought to be ruffled, and the lookout has stopped talking.
Brown water means sand close under us, and green water means room. Where it is smooth and ought to be rough, the bottom is holding the sea up.
The ship that carried Paul to Rome sounded and found twenty fathoms, and then fifteen, and then they dropped four anchors and prayed for daylight. I would sooner sound first and pray afterwards.
Put a man in the bow with the lead and feel your way

The weight goes down on its line and comes up and goes down again, and the man calls three fathoms, then two and a half, then two, then three again. The steersman follows the deep water round the bank like a man following a wall in the dark.
Stand out to deep water and go round
You give the brown water the width of a field and go round it in the green, which costs you a little of the day.
Hold your course: she draws little
She slides over with a hand's breadth to spare. The lookout watches the sand go by under the keel and says nothing until it is dark water again.
She stops quite gently, as if she had thought better of it, and you sit on the sand until the flood. The men climb out and walk round her on the bottom of the sea.

Bright daylight off a low coast; the sea ahead of the boat turning from green to a milky brown over a hidden bank; a man kneels in the bow lowering a weight on a line, the steersman leaning out to watch the colour of the water.
A mast on the shoal
A mast stands leaning out of the sea where no ship should be, with a rag of sail still on the yard and gulls sitting along it. Under it the sand shows pale through the water.
There is nobody on her, or nobody that I can see.
A mast like that is the best sea-mark there is, because it tells every ship not to come here.
They say half the ships in the British sea went down in one storm this last year. The sands will be full of marks like that one.
Stand in under oars and strip what the sea has left
The yard is still slung and the halyard still rove. You come away with a coil of good rope and the sound half of her sail, and nobody says whose they are.
The bank that took her nearly takes you as well. She touches and hangs there, and only comes off with the men over the side pushing, so you leave the mast to the gulls.
Give it a wide berth and remember where it stands
You pass it a long way off, and it will be the best sea-mark on this coast until the winter takes it down.
Row the length of the bank and look for her people
You take her slowly along the edge of the sand, with every man looking.

Grey daylight over shallow water; a wrecked ship's mast leaning out of the sea with a torn strip of sail on its yard and a row of gulls; pale sand visible under the water around it; the boat passing at a distance.
Men on the sand

Two men and a boy are standing on the last dry hump of the bank, up to their knees in the flood, and one of the men has an arm tied to his chest with a belt. They do not wave, because they have been waving since yesterday.
She struck in the night, and there were seven of us aboard her then. Take us off, for the love of God, because the tide is coming in!
That makes three more mouths, though one of them is a boy's, and we have the bread for it if nobody is greedy.
Take them off

They come aboard over the stern, too cold to help themselves, and sit where they are put. At the first landing they go ashore, and the man with the broken arm asks you twice for your name and your port, to be sure that he has them right.
Take them off, and keep the strongest as a hand
Two of them go ashore at the first landing. The third has no ship, no master and no reason to go home poor, so he takes an oar and says he will work his passage and then see.
Take them off, for what they saved from her
The dead master's purse was the one thing they had kept hold of, and now it is yours. They are alive, which is what they asked for, but they do not thank you.

A drowned sandbank at half tide under a cold clearing sky; two men and a boy standing knee-deep in the rising water, one with his arm bound to his chest, all three looking straight at the viewer; the boat's stem coming into the picture.
A drifting spar
A spar is floating a little way off the bow. It looks like a ship's yard, three fathoms of good pine with a tangle of rope trailing from one end.
It has not been in the water long, because the rope on it is still pale.
That was somebody's yard, and by now he is either cursing in a harbour or past all cursing.
Haul it aboard: timber is timber
It comes in over the gunwale streaming with water and is lashed along the thwarts. There will be a use for three fathoms of straight pine.
Look round for the ship it came from

There is no ship to be seen, but a cask is riding low in the water a little way off, tight and bunged, and when the men get it aboard it turns out to be ale. They take this as proof that God loves sailors.
A long time rowing in circles finds weed, a broken bailer, and one shoe.
Leave it: a drowned ship's gear is no gift
It drifts down the side and away astern, and Ravn watches it go and nods.
Open sea under broken cloud; a long pale spar floating in the foreground with a snarl of rope trailing from it; the boat coming up on it, the lookout leaning from the bow with a hooked pole.
Smoke on the shore
A column of smoke stands up from the shore to leeward, thick and dark at the foot, bending inland as it climbs. A second one is starting farther along.
Nobody keeps a watch on this coast for any king, so two smokes are either two salt-boilers or two farms burning, and from here they look just the same.

Since Charles set watchers at the river mouths, one smoke answers another on the Frankish shore whenever strange sails are seen. Then again it may only be salt-boilers, because from here they look just the same.
There were watchers on this coast once, in the old emperor's day. Now a smoke is a salter, or it is the Northmen, and nobody is paid to tell you which.
The second one is bigger than the first.
Stand out to sea and pass it wide
You put a good piece of water between yourself and whatever it is. By evening the smokes are two thin threads astern.
Stand in close enough to see what is burning
It is salt-boilers, with their peat stacks and clay pans, and men raking grey salt with their shirts off. They sell you a sack over the side for two pennies and want to know what day it is.
It is a hall burning, and the ships drawn up below it are not fishing boats. A man on the beach points at you, and you go about at once, but they do not trouble to launch after you.
Hold your course and keep a man watching astern
Nothing comes off that shore but smoke, and you never learn what it was.
A long low dune coast in clear daylight seen from the sea; two columns of dark smoke rising from behind the dunes and leaning inland; the boat in the foreground with the lookout pointing.
A fire in the night
There is a light low down on the black shore, steady and yellow and too big to be a hearth, and it does not move.
A fire on a headland at night may be a minster keeping its vigil, or a salter, or herdsmen. It tells you where the land is, and that is all it tells you.
The emperor has had the old Roman tower at Boulogne lit again for his ships. If that is what we are looking at, then we are in the narrow sea, and if it is not, then it is only a fire.
At midsummer your people light fires on the heights for one of your saints. If this is that night, there'll be more of them before morning.
Take it as a mark and steer by it till dawn
It burns all night in the same place. You keep it two hand-breadths off the bow, and at first light the coast is exactly where it should be.
Some time after midnight it goes out. You have been steering by a fire that somebody has now gone to bed from.
Keep well off a shore you cannot see
You stand out until the light is a spark, and wait for day with sea room all round you.
Close it and anchor under it
It is herdsmen, with a fire of driftwood on the beach and their cattle lying round it. You anchor off the sand and sleep to the sound of cows.
The fire was on a point with a reef off it, and she finds the reef before the anchor finds the bottom. She comes off again, but she has been hurt.

A black night sea and a blacker shore; one steady yellow point of fire low on the land, its reflection a thin broken line on the water; the boat's stern and steersman in dark outline in the foreground.
A sail
There is a sail on the edge of the sea, hull down, and at this distance nobody can say whether she is going your way or coming toward you.
She has one square sail and she sits low in the water, but something is moving along her side, and it could be oars.
She has one square sail and she is high in the side, and she rolls like a tub, so she must be a trader.
The reeve at Portland rode down to three strange ships to tell them the king's toll, because he took them for traders, and that was the last thing he ever took.
Two hundred Danish ships lay among the Frisian islands in the summer when their king Godfred was killed. One sail is not two hundred, but it is not none either.
Since Dorestat burned, a man looks at every sail twice.
Hold your course and watch her
You watch her all afternoon, and by evening she is a little smaller, and then she is gone, and you never learn her business.
Close her and speak her

She is a Frisian, four days out and deep in the water with querns and wine. Her master shouts across what wind he met and where, what the toll man is asking this year, and that his wife's brother is a fool, and then you part with a wave.
She alters toward you before you are near enough to hail, and will not answer when you do, and you do not wait to learn why. The men row until she gives up the chase at dusk.
Bear away and put the edge of the sea between you
You turn off your course until her sail sinks out of sight, which costs you a part of the day, though nobody aboard thinks it badly spent.
A wide empty sea in clear light; far off on the horizon a single small square sail; in the foreground the lookout standing on the stem with one arm round the forestay, shading his eyes.
A fishing boat
A fishing boat is lying to her lines ahead, with two men and a boy in her, a basket of fish between them and a net drying over an oar.
I have plaice and flounder, and an eel as long as the boy. I would rather have a knife than a penny for them, but I will take the penny.
I have herring too, because they came in so thick last night that you could have walked ashore on them.
You will not get in on this tide by the old way. The channel has gone north of the bank since the winter floods.
Buy fish for the pot, for a penny
One penny buys a basket of flatfish that are still moving. The men eat them half raw off the blade of a knife, and say it is the best meal of the voyage.
Ask him where the channel runs this year

He draws it on the water with the blade of an oar, showing you the bank, the cut to the north of it, and the stake with a rag on it where you turn. He says the channel moved in the winter floods, and that it will move again.
Hire him to take you in, for three pennies

He hands his own boat over to the boy, climbs aboard yours, and stands beside the steersman pointing with his chin, which the steersman bears well. You are over the bar before either of them has said twenty words.
A small open fishing boat on a quiet morning sea, two men and a boy in it, a wicker basket of flatfish and a net hung over an upright oar; the older man holding up a long eel toward the viewer.
Waiting on the tide
You are lying to your anchor and waiting for water. An English ship lies a short bowshot off doing the same, and her master, who has run out of things to look at, cups his hands round his mouth.
I have a thing aboard that fights wind and wave together and wins by lying still, and so have you. Name it for me, Frisian, and I will tell you what wool is fetching.
The English do love their riddles, and they would ask a drowning man what goes on one foot and has many ribs.
Take his riddle to think on
He says it through twice, so that you have it by heart. He is very pleased with it, the more so because he is sitting right on top of the answer.
Ask him for his news instead
He is six days from the Thames. He gives you the wind he had, a death in Kent that is of no use to you, and the price of wool whether you want it or not.
Wave, and go back to watching the tide
He waves back and looks round for somebody else to ask, while the tide makes at its own pace.
Two ships at anchor off a low shore in soft daylight, each with her sail furled; on the nearer one a broad English shipmaster with his hands cupped to his mouth, calling across the water.
A boat without oars
There is a hide boat ahead that is no bigger than a feeding trough, with three men in it and no oars. They are not waving to you, and one of them is singing.
We are on pilgrimage for the love of God, and we do not care where it takes us, because He will set us down wherever He wants us. You need not trouble yourselves about us.
They are Irish, and they put to sea with no oars and a week's food so that God can choose where they land. I had heard of it, but I never thought I would see it.
Three like these came ashore in Cornwall in a boat of two hides and a half, and went straight to King Alfred. They say he was glad of them.
Among my people a man who did this would be thought to be running from a killing.
Give them a sack of bread and a skin of water, and let them go where they are sent
They take the bread with both hands and bless the boat, the crew, and Ravn, who had not asked for it. Then the wind takes them on, and their singing carries a long way over the water.
Take them aboard to the next land

They come aboard as if it had been arranged. One of them reads the psalms aloud each morning and shows you how the letters make the sounds. At the first landing they thank you and walk inland without looking back.
Sail on: they asked for nothing
You leave them as you found them, and for a long time there is a speck astern and a thread of singing, and then there is only the sea.

Open sea in mild summer light; a tiny round-bellied hide boat with three tonsured men in rough cloaks sitting in it, no oars, one with his head back singing; the merchant boat coming up alongside, her crew staring.
A drowned man
Something pale turns over in a wave beside the boat and shows a face. It is a drowned man who has been some days in the sea, wearing a good wool tunic with a silver pin still at the shoulder.
A Christian is owed earth and a prayer. This one may not have been a Christian, but he is owed something all the same.
Leave the pin where it is, because the sea hasn't finished with him yet, and it knows what he was wearing.
Take him aboard for burial in holy ground, with a penny for the priest

He comes aboard heavier than a living man and is laid in the bow under a piece of sailcloth, where nobody will sit near him. The steersman says the prayers each evening, and at the first church you hand him over with a penny for the priest.
Say the prayer, weight him with a ballast stone, and give him back
The steersman says what he knows of the office, and the stone is tied to the man's ankles with a turn of good rope. He goes down feet first with the pin still at his shoulder.
Take the pin, and let him go
The pin is good silver, the weight of eight pennies. The body turns over again and drifts off astern, and nobody speaks to you until the evening meal, and then only about the wind.

Grey water close alongside the boat; a drowned man floating face up in a dark wool tunic with a round silver brooch at the shoulder; the crew leaning over the gunwale, one crossing himself, one turned away.
Birds going home
Birds are passing over the boat in ones and twos, low and straight, all the same way. Some carry small fish crosswise in their beaks.
A bird with a fish in its mouth is going home, and its home is a cliff. In the evening they fly to the land, and in the morning they fly out from it.
There are gulls too, higher up, and gulls always sleep ashore.
They tell of a man who took three ravens to sea to find land for him. The first flew back the way they had come and the third went on ahead, so he followed that one, but I forget what the second did.
Put her head where the birds are going
Before full dark there is a line of white under a darker line, and a smell of rock and droppings. It is a cliff, and under it lies the coast you wanted.
They were going to a rock, one bare stack in the open sea that is white with birds and has no land behind it. You have lost half a day learning where the birds live.
Have the steersman teach you the birds

He tells you that the ones with fish are going home, that gulls sleep ashore, and that a land bird at sea is lost and will go back by the shortest way. He says a man could cross the whole sea on birds, if he had the patience and a bird to ask.
Note their line and hold your own course
You have learned which hand the land is on, and that is worth having. The birds go on over the edge of the sea.

Evening light on an open sea; a loose string of small black-and-white seabirds flying low and straight across the picture, several with silver fish held crosswise in their beaks; below, the boat with her crew looking up.
A passenger
A small brown bird drops out of the sky onto the gunwale and sits there with its beak open, too spent to be afraid.
It weighs nothing at all, and I could close my whole hand round it.
Leave it be, for it's a guest that asks for nothing.
That is a swallow, and an early one. When the swallows cross, the sea is open for the year.
It is going south for the winter and has been blown off its road, and it has more sea ahead of it than we have.
Let it rest: a crumb of bread and a wet rag beside it
It sits on the gunwale with its eyes shut for as long as it takes to say a mass. Then it shakes itself, looks at each of you in turn, and goes, and the men watch it out of sight.
Cup it in your hands and warm it
Its heart goes like a small hammer. After a while it stops shaking, and when you open your hands it stays a moment longer than it has to.
It dies in your hands, quite quietly. The lookout takes it from you and puts it over the side as if it were something of his own.
Shoo it off the cargo
It flies a boat's length, comes back, and settles on the yard where you cannot reach it. The men find this funnier than it is.
Close view of the boat's gunwale in daylight with a small exhausted swallow perched on it, beak open; behind it, out of focus, the faces of two crewmen bending to look.
A raven on the yard
A raven comes out of nowhere, circles the mast twice, and settles on the yard. It looks down at the boat with one eye and then with the other.
Noah sent a raven out of the ark, and it never came back to tell him there was land. It is a faithless bird, and I would have it off my yard.
The High One keeps two of them, and they tell him everything that's done in the world. A raven on a ship is the best luck there is, so feed it!
Whatever it means, it did not come out of the sea. It came from land, and it knows where.
Feed it, as Ravn says
It takes a rind of cheese from Ravn's fingers as if it were owed. The steersman crosses himself and looks at the sea.
Drive it off, as the steersman says
A thrown rope's end sends it up off the yard, and it circles once, says something, and goes. Ravn does not speak for the rest of the watch.
Do neither: watch which way it flies when it goes
At noon it leaves, straight and unhurried, and you put the stem on the place where it went small. There is land under that place by evening.
It is still there at dusk, asleep with its head under its wing. Whatever it knows about land, it is keeping to itself.

Looking up the mast against a pale sky: a big black raven perched on the yard, head cocked, one eye on the viewer; below it the upturned faces of a grey-bearded Frisian frowning and an older Dane smiling.
A whale

A hundred fathoms off, the sea opens and a back comes up, black and wet and longer than the boat, and it is still coming. It blows, and its breath hangs in the air and drifts down on you, smelling of low tide.
It has not finished coming up.
Keep her as she goes, because a thing that size has no reason to notice us, and I would like to leave it that way.
The fishermen at home won't go after them. One blow of the tail and the boat's in the water, and they'd sooner catch a thing they can kill.
A Northman told King Alfred of whales fifty ells long, and said that six men had killed sixty sea-beasts in two days. The king had it written down, though nobody says that he believed it.
Hold your course and let it pass
It goes by down the side, a spear's length off, and it takes a long time about it. One eye the size of a bowl looks at the boat without any interest, and then the sea closes over it.
Bear away and give it the sea
You turn off and leave it a wide road. It blows twice more, farther off each time, and is gone.
Follow it: where a whale feeds there are fish
It is feeding on a shoal thick enough to darken the water. You dip baskets into the edge of what it leaves, and fill them.
It dives, and the tail comes up, stands a moment against the sky, and comes down a boat's length away. The wash fills her to the thwarts, and the men bail in silence.

A calm grey-green sea in daylight; the long black back of a great whale surfacing close beside the small boat, a plume of breath hanging above it; the crew frozen, one man with his oar lifted clear of the water.
Sea-pigs
There are porpoises off the bow, five or six small black backs rolling in a line, quick and quiet, and never showing more than a fin and a curve.
Those are sea-pigs, and the learned say that they play before a storm. I say that they play when they like and the wind comes when it likes, and now and then both happen on the same day.
Those are good eating, like pork that's been to sea.
Take them as luck, and watch
They keep station off the bow for a while, rolling one after another like a wheel turning. Then, all at once, they are somewhere else.
Take them as a warning: stow and lash for wind
Everything loose is chocked and roped, so if the wind comes you are ready for it, and if it does not, the steersman will say that the pigs were only playing.
Try for one with a hook and a line
By luck more than skill the hook takes the last of them behind the fin. It is hauled in thrashing, and there is red meat for three days.
They are faster than anything with a hook has a right to expect. The line comes back wet, and the hook with nothing on it.
A light sea in sunshine; a line of five small dark porpoise backs curving out of the water just ahead of the boat's stem; a crewman leaning over the bow, pointing and grinning.
Seals on a bank
The tide has left a long sandbank bare, and it is covered in seals, sixty or eighty of them lying there like sacks. As the boat comes abreast of them, every head lifts at once.
A bank with seals on it dries out at every tide, and knowing that is worth more than the seals are.
Seal hide makes the best rope a ship can carry, and the worst smell.
There are pups too, small ones, down at the water's edge.
Pass quietly and mark where the bank lies
You go by under oars at a distance they will bear. The steersman fixes the bank against two marks on the shore and says them over twice.
Clap your hands and watch them go
The whole bank empties into the water like a spilled basket, and the men laugh. Then eighty heads come up in a row and watch you until you are out of sight.
Land two men with clubs for skins and oil
The men are among them before the old ones have turned round. It is quick, ugly work, and you leave with a bundle of skins rolled wet in the bow.
The seals are in the water before the keel touches, but the boat is on the sand on a falling tide, and it takes every man a long, cold while to get her off.
Low tide under a wide pale sky; a long bare sandbank crowded with grey seals lying close together, every head raised and turned toward the boat as she passes along the edge of the bank.
The sea boiling
The sea ahead is boiling. Gannets fall into it from mast height with their wings folded, one after another, and the water between them is thick and silver.
It is herring, and the whole sea has come up to the top with them.
There are a dozen boats or more on the far side of it, and nobody in them is looking at us.
Dip the baskets: fresh fish tonight
The bailer comes up full of fish at every dip. The men eat herring until they cannot look at herring, and the gannets go on falling all round you.
Salt a cask of them down with a sack of your salt
It takes a sack of your salt and the spare cask, with the men gutting the fish with their thumbs. By dusk there is a barrel of salt herring aboard that cost you nothing but the salt.
Sail through: you carry cargo, not a net
She goes through the shoal with fish knocking against the planks. A gannet hits the water close enough to wet the steersman, who says nothing.
Autumn daylight on a lively sea; the water ahead of the boat seething silver with fish, white gannets plunging into it like thrown spears, a scatter of small fishing boats beyond.
Geese coming in
Geese are coming in off the sea: one long wavering line after another, high up, calling to each other the whole way.
They are coming down from the north for the winter, and when the geese come in, sensible men go home.
The goose is a wise bird, for it knows when to leave a cold country, and it carries no cargo.
Take the warning: finish this run and lay her up
You say it aloud, and the men's shoulders come down a little. There will be one more landfall, and after that a roof, a fire, and the boat up on the bank.
One more voyage: prices are best when few ships sail
The men hear you, and although nobody argues, nobody sings for the rest of the day either.
Watch them over and say nothing yet
They pass for most of an evening, line after line, until the sky is empty and it is suddenly much colder.
A cold autumn dusk at sea, the sky banded orange and grey; long wavering skeins of geese crossing high overhead toward a dark line of land; the boat small below, her crew looking up.
Something in the bread
A sack of ship's bread has a hole in one corner the size of a thumb, a trail of crumbs, and droppings in the fold. Something came aboard at the last landing and has been living well.
It is a rat, because I saw its tail go under the floor timbers.
It's eaten better than we have, just look at the size of those droppings!
It is only one rat, and with luck it will still be only one rat in a month. I have seen boats where the bread walked about by itself.
Shift every sack and hunt it out
It breaks from under the last sack and runs the length of the boat, and the lookout gets it with the bailer. It goes over the side by the tail, to everybody's satisfaction.
It is somewhere under the floor timbers where no hand will go. By the time you give it up, a second sack has been opened from below.
Sling the bread in a net from the yard
From now on the bread swings over everybody's head and has to be lowered for every meal. The rat goes hungry, and so do the men, a little.
Let it be: one rat eats little
It eats little, and spoils more than it eats. Before the next port a whole sack has gone grey and is thrown to the gulls.

Inside the boat among the cargo: a gnawed sack of hard loaves with crumbs spilling from one corner; the youngest hand on his knees peering under the floor timbers, bailer raised, the older men watching with folded arms.
Spring ice

There is white on the water ahead, and it is not foam. It is ice floes, grey-white and rotten at the edges, drifting in a loose field with dark lanes between them and knocking together with a sound like wooden bowls.
That is spring ice, which is too rotten to bear a man and still hard enough to open a plank, so it is the worst of both.
The Svear drive sledges over this sea at midwinter and sail it at midsummer, and this is neither of those.
There are seals lying out on the far floes.
Lie off and wait for the wind to open a lane
You lie to the oars outside the edge of it. Toward evening the wind shifts, the floes begin to move apart, and a road of black water opens as if a door had been unbarred.
Work through the lanes under oars, with a man fending off
The lookout stands in the bow with an oar and calls each floe before it comes, which takes half a day and all of his voice. On the far side the water is open.
A floe the size of a threshing floor turns under the bow, and the planking takes it with a sound that nobody likes. A plank has started, and there is a long way still to go.
Go round by the open water
It adds a day to the voyage, and the men grumble as they have every right to, but the planks stay where the shipwright put them.

A cold bright spring day on a dark sea scattered with flat grey-white ice floes, narrow black lanes of water between; the boat nosing into the edge of the field, a man standing in the bow with an oar held like a spear.
Ice on the stream
Ice is coming down the stream in plates the size of tables, turning slowly and grinding along the bank. The reeds are stiff with frost, and every mooring post wears a white cap.
That is drift ice, and it takes the tar off her first and then the plank under the tar. She ought to be up on the bank with a roof over her.
Last winter they drove loaded carts across the Rhine for thirty days together. Next to that, this is a kindness.
Haul her out at the next landing and wait for a thaw
She is dragged up over the frozen mud on rollers and chocked. The men find a roof and a fire, and the ice goes on down the river without you.
Keep the middle of the stream, with poles out to fend off
The plates knock and turn aside. It is slow, cold work, and by dusk you are below the worst of it with the tar still on her.
One plate rides up on another and both come down on the bow, and the men fend them off with their hands in the water. Afterwards there is a seam that drips.

A winter river under a white sky; plates of grey ice turning in the brown current, frosted reeds along the bank and snow-capped mooring posts; the boat in midstream with two men holding poles out against the ice.
No night
It is the middle of the night and it is not dark. The whole north sky is the colour of a pearl, and the sun's glow is walking along under the edge of the sea from the west side to the east.
Bede the Englishman wrote that at midsummer a watcher at midnight cannot tell the end of evening from the beginning of morning. He lived at Jarrow, and north of Jarrow it is plainer still.
North of my country it doesn't set at all. The people there get nothing done for a month, and they call it summer.
Irish hermits who spent a summer in the far island say that a man can pick the lice out of his shirt at midnight there, and hermits would know.
Sail on through it
Nobody sleeps much. The men sit with their backs to the cargo and watch the glow go round the north from one hand to the other, and at some point it is morning without ever having been night.
Use the light: set the men to mending gear
Needles, twine and tallow come out, and every weak seam in the sail is doubled and every chafed rope turned end for end, by a light that costs nothing. The men would have preferred to sleep.
Sleep, and give the oar to the lookout
You wake to the same grey light, the same course, and a lookout very pleased with himself.
You wake to find the glow on the wrong side of the boat. He has steered half a circle by a sky that looks the same all the way round.

Midnight at midsummer: a calm sea under a luminous pearl-grey northern sky with a band of pale gold along the horizon, no stars; the boat under sail in soft twilight, the crew awake and looking north.
Fire in the north
The whole north sky is alight. Long pale curtains hang and shift there, green at the hem, and now and then a red spear runs up through them and fades, all without any sound.
They saw this over Northumbria in the spring before the heathen came to Lindisfarne, and the English called it fiery dragons.
The English saw lights and then the Northmen came, and now every light in the sky is a dragon. I have seen this a dozen times and been robbed once.
At home it comes with the frost. The old people say it means cold, and they're right, because you only see it when it's cold.
Tell the men it is weather, and to mind the sheets
You say it as if you knew, and after a while they believe you, or pretend to, and go back to their places.
They do not believe you, and the lookout says that the English did not believe it either, and look what came to Lindisfarne.
Let the steersman lead a prayer
He says the Our Father slowly and the men say it after him, while Ravn watches the sky. When they have finished the lights are still there, but they are easier to look at.
Ask the lookout what the English wrote of it

He has it almost word for word from an English hand he once shared an oar with: sheets of light, whirlwinds and fiery dragons, and then a famine, and then the heathen men. He tells it well, and nobody thanks him for it.

A clear cold night at sea; green and pale-red curtains of light hanging in the northern sky and reflected faintly on the black water; the boat in dark outline, the crew standing, one man with his hands joined.
The sea burning
The sea is burning tonight: every oar-stroke leaves a hole of green fire, the wake is a lit road behind the boat, and a fish darting under the keel draws a bright line like a falling star.
Look at my hand, all of you, look at my hand!
Warm nights at the end of summer. It does no harm and it means nothing, and I have never once been able to stop watching it.
Old people at home say it's the drowned, lighting their way. I don't put my hand in it, all the same.
Let the men trail their hands in it
Each man in turn puts an arm over the side and pulls it out dripping light. The lookout writes his name on the sea with a finger, or says that he does, since he cannot write.
Use it: every bank and every boat will show tonight
The steersman has seen it before you say it: every bank breaks in a line of pale fire tonight, and can be seen a long way off. He threads her between them without a word.
Order them back to their places
They go back to their places, but all night, whenever an oar dips, every head turns to look at the hole of light it leaves.
A warm dark late-summer night; the sea black, but the boat's wake and each oar-splash glowing cold green; a young crewman holding up a hand that drips light, his face lit from below.
A feast day at sea
It is a feast day, and the nearest altar is a day's sail off. On shore the bells are going and nobody is working.
It is a high day, and on shore the bells have been going since dawn and nobody has lifted a tool.
It is a summer feast, with the nights at their shortest, and on shore they are lying in the new grass with nothing to do, while we have a wet rope and a cheese.
It is Saint Mary's day in harvest, when every reaper in Francia has put down his sickle, and here we are working.
It is the mass of Michael, the angel who weighs the souls, and from here the year turns toward the dark.
It is a feast in the slaughter month, and when the wind comes off the land you will smell the smoke from every yard.
It is Christ's mass and we are at sea, which means that somebody has made a bad plan.
My gods ask for a feast three times in the year and don't mind where I am when I keep it, but yours keep a longer list than that.
Keep it: no work but the sailing, a prayer, and the best of the food
The steersman says the prayer for the day, the cheese is cut thick, and nobody is set to scrape or mend. It is not a feast, but it is nearer to one than this boat usually comes.
Keep it with ale: broach a cask
A cask of the cargo is broached and written off. By evening Ravn is teaching the lookout a song the steersman says no Christian should know on such a day, and joins in the second time round.
A day like any other: carry on
The work goes on, and the steersman does his share of it without a word and then says the prayer by himself in the stern, loud enough to be heard.

A fair day at sea; the crew sitting idle among the cargo round a thick-cut wheel of cheese and a loaf, the steersman with his head bowed and one hand raised in blessing, the Dane leaning back against the mast, watching.
A fast day and no fish
It is a fast day, which means no flesh, and in Lent no cheese either, and there is no fish aboard. What there is is bread, and a wheel of cheese that everyone is carefully not looking at.
Bread and water never killed a man in one day. It is the second day that does it.
I'll eat the cheese for all of you and carry the sin of it myself, since I've plenty of room for it.
In Saxony the king's law takes a man's head for eating flesh in Lent. We are not in Saxony, of course, and I only mention it.
Keep the fast: bread and water

It is bread, and water from the cask, and the cheese is left where it is. The men are hungry and rather pleased with themselves, and Ravn fasts too, out of manners, and says it is no worse than a bad day's fishing.
Put lines over the side and let God provide
The lines bring up three codling and a gurnard inside the time it takes to say a psalm. The steersman says it is a plain answer to prayer, and Ravn says that nobody told the fish what day it was.
Nothing bites, and the steersman says that the sea must be keeping the fast too.
Eat the cheese, and confess it ashore
The wheel is cut and everyone eats, and nobody meets anyone else's eye. The steersman takes the smallest piece and makes it last.

The crew sitting round a single flat loaf and a water cask in grey daylight, an uncut wheel of cheese on a sack between them; every man looking somewhere else, the Dane looking straight at the cheese.
A weeping seam

There is more water over the floor timbers than spray accounts for. The youngest hand, bailing, has found where: a lap below the waterline on the steering side is weeping, a thread of sea running down the inside of the plank.
A rivet has worked loose, or the wool has gone out of the lap. It is nothing yet, but then every one of them is nothing yet.
It is cold, wherever it is coming from, and my feet found it before the rest of me did.
Drive tarred wool into the lap from inside
A twist of tarred wool goes in with a wooden wedge and the back of an axe, and the thread of water thins to a sweat and then to nothing.
The wool goes in and the water comes round it. Whatever has let go is on the outside, under the waterline, where no hand can reach it.
Open a barrel of your own tar and do it properly

There is no heating tar in an open boat, but cold tar and wool, worked in with a thumb and wedged, will do. The seam is tight before the barrel is headed up again, though it is no longer a barrel that you can sell.
Set a man to bail and carry on to port
One man bails a little in every watch, which is no great thing, because the water comes in at the pace of a slow thought and so far it goes out faster.

Inside the hull, low down between two frames: a thin bright thread of water running down the dark tarred planking from an overlapping seam; a young man's hand with a wooden bailer beside it, bilge water over the floor timbers.
The leak gains
The leak has grown, so that one man bailing no longer keeps it down, and even with two at it the water still creeps up the frames between scoops. The lowest of the cargo is standing in it.
With a hand's depth of loose water in an open boat she rolls like a drunk man, so either we stop this or we stop sailing.
I'm bailing as fast as I can, and there's a second bailer lying there if anyone has a hand free.
Beach her on the first sand and get at it from outside

She is run up on a falling tide and heeled over on her bilge, and the started rivet is there for anyone to see. A new rove, a hammer and wool put it right, and the flood lifts her off the richer by one mended plank and the poorer by a day.
Heel her at sea and patch it from over the side
With the cargo shifted to one side the bad lap comes up out of the water, and a man hung over the gunwale by his belt drives a wedge and wool into it between seas until it holds.
She will not heel far enough, and the man over the side takes a sea in the face for every blow he strikes. The water gains, and the bottom sacks are spoiled.
All hands bail by turns, and run for port
They bail in pairs, by the count of two hundred, and then change over, and she makes the land with the water no higher than it was. The men fall asleep where they sit.
The water gains a finger in every watch. You reach the land in the end, with the men grey in the face and the bottom of the cargo afloat.

The boat low in the water on a grey sea, two men bailing hard side by side with water flying from the scoops, sacks in the bottom of the boat dark and half awash; the steersman looking toward a distant strip of beach.
Daylight through the sail
Daylight shows through the sail where it should not: a hand's length of seam has let go near the foot, and the cloth on either side of it is working with every gust.
A wool sail gives you a year's warning, and then no warning at all.
Give somebody the needle now, or you'll be giving him the two halves later, and don't let it be me, because you've not seen my sewing.
Lower the yard and stitch it now
The yard comes down, the needle and the waxed twine come out, and the steersman sews it with a seam flat enough for a shirt. Part of a fair wind is lost over it, but the sail is not.
Cut a patch from the sailcloth in the hold
A bolt of the cargo is opened, and a doubled patch goes over the whole foot of the sail, which is stronger there now than it was when it was new. The rest of the bolt, though, is no longer for sale.
Leave it till port: the wind is fair
The wind is fair and the sail holds. Each gust opens the seam the width of another thread, and everybody aboard has stopped looking at it.

Looking up at the square sail from the deck with the sun behind it: a short bright slit of daylight in the dark cloth near the lower edge; the old Dane below, squinting up, a needle held between his teeth.
The sail splits
With a crack like a dropped plank the sail splits from the foot to the yard. Two halves stream out downwind, thrashing, and the boat falls off into the trough.
Mind your heads!
Get it down before it beats itself to rags, and after that we row, and after that we sew.
Get it down, hold her head to the sea, and sew
Two men at the oars keep her head up while the other two sew, wet through, with the sail across their knees. It takes most of a night, and in the morning it is one sail again, and an ugly one.
Set the sound half on the spar you picked up

The drifting yard you hauled aboard is the right length for half a sail. Lashed up and hoisted, it makes a small, mean, serviceable rag that takes you in. The steersman says he knew there would be a use for it.
Run on under what is left of it
The two halves hold by the head-rope and pull like two small sails. It is not seamanlike, and it gets you there.
The yard comes down with the last of the sail and catches a man across the shoulder, though nothing is broken that will not mend. You sew the sail in the morning with one pair of hands fewer.
A fresh grey day; the square sail torn in two from bottom to top, both halves flying out to leeward like flags, ropes whipping; the crew ducking, the steersman shouting with one arm flung up.
The cargo moves
On a hard roll something heavy slides in the hold and fetches up against the lee side with a thump that everyone feels in their feet. She does not come all the way back upright.
The cargo has moved, so she is lying on her ear, and the next sea will find that out.
It is the quernstones, and one of them is up on its edge against the planking.
Bring her head to the wind and restow
It takes four men, a lever and a good deal of language to get it back where it belongs, and this time it is wedged and lashed, and she stands up straight again.
Put the stones that moved over the side
A pair of querns goes over the lee gunwale and down. It is twelve pennies on the bottom of the sea, and the boat is the right way up.
Trim her with the men's weight and sail on
Three men sit out on the high side and she comes back nearly level. It will do until the sea goes down.
The next sea finds the low side and comes in over it green. She lives through it, but the bottom tier of the cargo is under water before it can be bailed.
The boat heeled hard over on a windy sea, her lee gunwale almost in the water; inside, sacks and a pair of dark round quernstones slid down against the low side, two men scrambling toward them.
A cask is weeping
One of the wine casks is weeping at a stave. There is a red stain down its side, a smell over the whole boat, and three men have found reasons to be standing next to it.
It'd be a sin to let it run into the bilge. I'm thinking only of the cargo, mind.
Wine is the lord's drink and the altar's, and that is the whole of the reason they want it.
Drive the hoops down and stop it with tallow
The hoops are driven a finger's width, the stave is rubbed with tallow, and the stain dries. The three men go back to their places with the look of men who have been to a burial.
Draw a jug for the men before you stop it

One jug goes round twice. It is Rhenish, and none of them has tasted the like outside a lord's hall. Then the hoops are driven down, and from now on the cask will sound a little hollow to a buyer who knocks on it.
It is leaking anyway: let them finish the cask

A cask of wine is a great deal for five men, but they do their best with it. In the morning the sea is very bright and nobody wants to talk about it, and Ravn says his people have a verse about what a man should not carry on a journey.
Among the cargo: a stout wine cask with a dark red trickle down its staves, three sailors standing close around it with studied innocence, one holding an empty wooden jug behind his back.
A man in the sea
A sea lifts the bow, the youngest hand is standing where he should be sitting, and then he is not in the boat. His head comes up a spear's cast astern with his mouth open.
He is no Breca to swim his way out of it, so get her round!
The water is cold enough to stop a man's arms in the time it takes you to count a hundred, so you'd better count fast.
Down sail, out oars, and pull back for him
It is the slow way and the sure one. By the time the oars reach him he has stopped shouting and is only holding his face out of the water. He comes in over the gunwale like a sack of wet grain.
Throw him the bailer on its line
The bailer lands an arm's length from his head. He gets both hands on it and is hauled in hand over hand, swearing, which is the best sound anyone has heard all day.
The line falls short, and he goes under reaching for it. It takes the oars after all, and longer than it should. He is the wrong colour when he comes aboard.
Throw him an oar to hold, and bring her round under sail
He gets an arm over the oar. She comes round in a wide circle, the steersman judging it to a boat's length, and two men lift him in as she passes.
She will not come round fast enough in this sea. The second pass finds him, still on the oar, with his eyes shut.

A lumpy grey sea seen from the boat's stern; a boy's head and one raised arm in the water a little way behind, in the white of the wake; in the foreground the steersman hauling on the steering oar and a hand flinging a wooden bailer on a line.
He has stopped shivering

The man you pulled out of the sea is lying in the bottom of the boat with his knees drawn up to his chin. He has stopped shivering, which the steersman says is worse than shivering. His lips are the colour of slate.
The cold gets inside a man and stays there after he is dry. I have seen them stand up, say they feel well, and fall down dead.
Strip him, wrap him in every dry cloak, and put a man on each side
It takes three cloaks and two warm bodies and half a day. Toward evening he begins to shake again and then to complain, and the steersman says that he will live.
Broach a cask of ale and get some into him
He swallows the first cup because he is told to and the second because he wants it. The colour comes back into his face.
He cannot keep it down, so he is no worse for it but no better either, and the cask is open now.
Put him back on an oar to warm himself
He rows like a man asleep for a long while. Then the sweat comes, and he wakes up, and asks what everyone is staring at.
He takes six strokes, says quite clearly that he feels well, and falls forward over the loom of the oar, and he does not get up again. The steersman had seen it happen before.

The bottom of the boat in flat grey light: a young man curled on his side under a heap of cloaks, face grey, lips dark; another man lying close against his back for warmth, the steersman kneeling with a hand on his forehead.
A man with fever
One of the men did not get up for his turn at the oar. He is hot to the touch, his teeth are knocking together, and he says the boat is full of people he knows.
It is a fever. The old men say to bleed him and the priest says to pray, and whichever of those we do, he rows for nobody today.
In the marsh country it comes on every third day and goes again, like a toll man. This has the look of it.
Rest him in the stern under a cloak, with water
He sleeps a day and a night and wakes thin, sour and himself. He wants to know who has been using his bailer.
He is no better in the morning. He takes water and loses it, and talks to his mother.
Keep him at his oar: he can sweat it out
He rows with his eyes shut and the sweat running off him, and by evening the heat has gone out of him with it. Nobody is more surprised than he is.
He falls off the thwart at the third change of the watch. The other men lift him into the stern without being told, and look at you.
Put in to the nearest landing and find him a roof
A farm above the landing takes him in. Two days under a roof with broth and a fire do what the boat could not. You lose the days and keep the man.
A man lying in the stern of the boat under a brown cloak, eyes half open and bright, sweat on his face, one hand reaching at nothing; his oar lying idle on the thwart; a grey sea, a low sky.
The sick man is worse
The sick man is worse, and he no longer knows the boat. He has not kept water down since yesterday, and the others have moved their sleeping places away from him without anyone telling them to.
It is the landing now, or the cloak and the stone. I would rather it was the landing.
Make for the nearest roof, whatever shore it is
You give up the course and run for the first smoke you see, where strangers carry him up from the beach on a hurdle. He lies a week under their roof and he lives, and it costs you the week.
Bleed him, as the old men say
Ravn opens a vein in the arm with the small knife and lets a cupful go into the bailer. That night the fever breaks in a sweat that soaks the cloak. Nobody can say that the one caused the other.

He is too weak to spare the blood, and he dies before morning, quietly, with the steersman holding his hand. He is sewn into his cloak with a ballast stone and given to the sea, with such prayers as the boat knows.
Vow an offering at the next altar, and nurse him as you can
You say the vow aloud so that the men hear it. On the third day he asks for bread. The steersman says you had better remember what you promised.
He is no better and no worse: he lies between. The vow stands, and the men take turns to wet his mouth.

Dusk at sea; the sick man lying very still in the stern with his eyes shut, the steersman holding his wrist; the other men sitting as far forward as the boat allows, looking back; a thin smoke on a far shore.
Bad water
One of the water casks has gone bad, and what comes out of it is green, smells like a harbour at low tide, and has things in it that swim. The other casks are not full.
A man can row for two days with no food in him, but with no water he cannot row for one.
It'll not kill us, so long as you hold your nose and think of ale while you drink it.
Put in for water at the first stream
A beck runs down the beach under a low cliff. The casks are scoured with sand and filled, and the men drink until they are as tight as drums.
Ration it: a cup a man, morning and evening
It is a cup at dawn and a cup at dusk, measured out by the steersman with every man watching the level. It can be done, though it is not pleasant and it makes for short tempers.
Broach a cask of the ale instead
A cask of ale that was meant for market becomes ship's stores, and the men bear the hardship without complaint.
A water cask with its bung out, tipped over a wooden cup; the water in the cup green and cloudy; the old Dane holding the cup at arm's length and looking into it with one eyebrow raised.
The last of the water
The cask is down to the dregs. Tongues are thick, lips are split, and nobody has spat over the side all day.
We land at the first green we see.
Land wherever there is green, and dig above the tide line
Behind the first dune Ravn digs with an oar-blade to the depth of his arm. The hole fills slowly with water that is brown, tastes of roots, and is the best any of them has ever drunk.
Spread the sail for dew and rain, and hold on
A grey shower crosses you before dawn, and the sail, spread like a trough, runs a cask half full of water that tastes of wool and tar, which nobody complains about.
No rain comes, and the dew wets the sail and nothing else. By the next evening two men cannot swallow bread.
Hail the first boat you see and buy water, for two pennies
A fishing boat comes by with a skin of water under the stern thwart. The man in it will not take silver for water, so he takes it for the skin instead.
The sea is empty all that day, so you keep your two pennies and your thirst with them.
Four men slumped in the boat under a hard bright sky, lips cracked, one holding an upturned empty cup; a flat glittering sea all round and, very far off, a thin green line of shore.
Two hands on the oar

The lookout says the steersman has let her fall off to leeward all morning. The steersman says a boy who has steered nothing bigger than a ferry should keep his eyes on the sea and his mouth for eating. Both have a hand on the steering oar.
I can hold her closer to the wind than that, because I have watched him do it for two summers and I know how it is done.
The oar is mine for as long as I am aboard, and that is not pride talking, it is how boats stay the right way up.
Back the steersman: the oar is his
You only have to say it once. The boy takes his hand away and goes forward to the bow, where he looks at the sea very hard for the rest of the day.
Give the boy a spell at the oar under the steersman's eye
He steers a straight wake for the length of a watch, with the steersman sitting behind him saying nothing at all. When he hands the oar back he is a hand's breadth taller.
He lets her come up too far, the sail goes aback with a bang, and a rope takes the skin off a man's palm. The steersman takes the oar back without a word, since he does not need one.
Say nothing and let them settle it
They settle nothing between them. The steersman keeps the oar, the boy keeps his opinion, and the two of them stop speaking, which in a boat this size is a silence that everybody hears.

The stern of the boat: a grey-bearded steersman and a boy of eighteen face to face, each with one hand clamped on the tiller of the side rudder, neither giving way; the other men pretending to look at the sea.
It comes to hands
It has come to hands at last: the boy has a split lip, the steersman has him by the hair over the gunwale, and the boat is steering herself.
Among my people this is settled on an island, with a cloak pegged down to stand on. There's no island here, and the cloak's yours.
Take the oar yourself and order them apart
They let go of each other, and each goes to his own end of the boat. You steer for the rest of the watch, not very well, and nobody remarks on it.
Dock them both a day's share for the ship's peace
A day's share each, to be drunk by the others at the next landing. They are united for the first time in a week, in thinking it unjust.
Broach a cask of ale and make them clasp hands over it
They clasp hands across the cask, stiffly, and drink. By the second cup the steersman is showing the boy how to feel the wind on the back of his neck.
They drink, since it is there to be drunk, but they do not clasp hands. The cask is lighter for it and the boat is no quieter.

The same stern, a moment later: the steersman gripping the boy by the hair and forcing him back over the gunwale, the boy's lip bleeding and his fist drawn back; the steering oar swinging free, the Dane watching with interest.
Asleep at the oar

You wake in the dead of the night to a different motion. The boat is lying across the sea with the sail slatting, and the man at the steering oar is asleep on his feet with his arm hooked over the tiller.
Whose watch is it? No, do not tell me whose it is, tell him.
Take the oar yourself till dawn, and let him sleep
You ease him down onto the cargo without waking him, and steer until the east goes grey. In the morning he knows what happened, and he works like two men all that day and never mentions it.
Wake him with a bailer of sea water
He comes up gasping, sees the sail, sees you, and has her back on her course before he has finished coughing. It is a story against him by the morning meal.
Rouse the whole boat and shame him
Every man is woken to look at him. Nobody sleeps on watch again this voyage, and nobody sings either.

Deep night, a little starlight; a man standing asleep at the stern with his arm hooked over the tiller and his chin on his chest, the sail hanging and flapping; the merchant sitting up among the cargo, just woken, looking at him.
Nothing but sea
There has been no land on any side since yesterday. The sea is the same in every direction, the wind has shifted twice in the night, and it is near noon with the sun out.
At noon the sun stands in the south, and a man's shadow is the shortest it will be all day. If you miss it, you wait for tomorrow.
In the Greeks' sea the sun went dark for seventeen days, the year they blinded their emperor, and ships lost themselves in open water, or so a trader told it at Dorestat.
Take the noon shadow yourself, as he taught you
You stand an oar upright on the thwart and watch its shadow shorten, stop, and begin to grow. Where it pointed when it stopped is north. The steersman, asked, says it will do.
Have the steersman find south, and show you how

He stands the boy against the mast and watches his shadow on the thwart get shorter, stop, and start to grow. That is south, he says, and the one honest moment of the day. He puts her on her course by it.
A cloud comes across at the wrong moment and stays. He shows you the way of it all the same, with an oar and an imagined shadow, and steers by his best guess.
Keep the wind on the same cheek and trust it
The wind has held where it was after all. Toward evening the right piece of coast lifts out of the sea, and you are free to say you knew it would.
The wind has gone round with the sun and taken you with it. By evening there is still no land, and the steersman is being very polite.

High noon on an empty sea, no land anywhere; a boy standing with his back against the mast while the steersman crouches, watching the boy's short shadow on the thwart and marking its end with his thumb.
The ship-star
It is a clear night with no moon, and the stars are so thick that the mast seems to stir them. One of them, low in the north, has hardly moved since dusk.
The English call it the ship-star, and everything else goes round it like cattle round a post. If you keep it over one shoulder you are going the same way all night.
We call the seven bright ones beside it the Wagon. It goes round all night and never unloads.
Steer by it through the night
You keep it over the same shoulder all night, and the Wagon wheels slowly round it. At dawn the land comes up where it was meant to.
