Some time after midnight a cloud as wide as the sea eats the north. You steer by the feel of the wind until it gives the star back.
Have the steersman show you the star and the Wagon
Seven bright stars make a wagon with its pole. The two at the back of the cart point to the one that hardly moves. He makes you find it three times from nothing before he is satisfied.
Lie to until daylight
The sail comes down and she lies quiet under the stars. It is a waste of a fair night, and nobody runs onto anything.

A moonless night crowded with stars over a calm black sea; the Plough standing on its handle in the northern sky with one steady star beyond it; the boat under sail, the steersman's arm raised and pointing.
The wrong headland
Dawn shows land where land should be, but the headland is the wrong shape: it is too low, with a notch in it that nobody knows, and a river mouth where the steersman's memory has a beach.
The sea has carried us along the shore in the night, and whether it was up it or down it I cannot say. The land is where it should be, so it is I who am wrong.
There is a roof over there. It might be a church or it might be a barn, but it is something with a roof on it.
Coast along until a mark you know comes up

Half a day along the shore a low point opens that the steersman has seen before, with a minster on it he can put a name to. He says the sea carried you a long way in the night, and he says it as though that were the sea's fault.
Land a man to ask where you are

A shepherd tells him the name of the place, the name of the next one, and how far you are from where you thought you were, and then laughs for some time. Your man comes back along the beach with a red face.
Your man finds a cold hearth, a dog on a rope, and nobody who will come out of the reeds to speak to a stranger off a ship, which tells you something about this shore as well.
Trust your first reckoning and stand on
The next point is the one you know. You were less lost than the steersman feared, and he takes it as a personal kindness.
The coast runs on, strange, all day. At dusk you put about and go back the whole way you came, against the wind.

A grey dawn; the boat close under a low unfamiliar headland with a notch in its skyline and a small river running out beside it, one thatched roof behind the dunes; the steersman standing, frowning at the land with his arms folded.
The smell of land
The wind has come round off a land you cannot see, and it has brought the land with it: cut hay, peat smoke, cattle. The men lift their heads like dogs.
That is hay, and it is half a day off and no more, upwind of us. A man can find a coast with his nose if the wind lets him.
There's peat smoke under the hay, which is somebody's supper! It's a strange thing to smell another man's hearth from out at sea.
Turn up into the smell and close the land
You follow it like a hound, a little this way and a little that, and the smell thickens until there is a line of dunes at the end of it.
The wind shifts and takes the hay with it. You are left steering at a smell that is no longer there.
Hold your course: you know now which side the land lies
You keep on as you were. For a while longer the boat sails through somebody's hay harvest, and then it is only sea again.
A summer night at sea, dark blue, a thin moon; all the men in the boat with their faces lifted and turned the same way into the wind, eyes half shut, like hounds; no land in sight.
A weir in the channel

There are stakes across the shallows ahead, with wattle woven between them in a long V and a basket at the point. It is somebody's fish weir, built farther out into the channel than it has any right to be.
My father built it, and his father cut the stakes for it. The channel is over on that side, and there is room in it for a careful man.
Every year they build them a little farther out. One day a man will walk across this river on fish baskets.
Go round by the narrow water, slowly
There is room, as he said, for a careful man. The oars on one side touch his stakes, and the oars on the other touch the reeds.
Buy eels from his basket, for two pennies
He tips them into your bailer alive, a knot of them, for two pennies. Split and laid over a fire on the bank that night, they are worth four.
Push through the end of the wattle: she will ride over it
The last stake bends under the keel and springs up again behind you. He shouts something about your mother, but nothing is broken.
Three stakes go, and a length of wattle with them. He is alongside in his logboat before you are a bowshot downstream, naming the price of his father's work, and he has two sons with him.

A broad slow river between reed beds in daylight; a V-shaped fence of stakes and woven wattle running out from the bank with a wicker basket at its point; a man in a logboat beside it, one hand on a stake, watching the merchant boat come down on him.
The stream against you
The stream is against you, and there is not wind enough to stem it. On the bank a man with two oxen is watching you lose ground, and he has a rope coiled on his shoulder.
It is a penny to the next bend and two to the landing, and it is all one to the oxen which you choose.
A boat going upstream is a cart with no wheels. Somebody pulls it, or it stays where it is.
Pay him two pennies to tow you
The rope is made fast forward, the oxen lean into it, and the bank begins to go by at the pace of a man walking. The crew sit with their hands in their laps and watch the country.
Put two of your own men on the bank with the rope
Two men go ashore with the rope over their shoulders while two stay aboard to keep her off the bank, and they change over at every bend. It gets you there, and nobody has breath to spare for talking.
Anchor and wait for a wind
You lie under the bank and watch the stream go by. The ox man waits too, a little way off, in case you change your mind.

A river bank in flat windless daylight; a man in a short cloak standing with two yoked oxen and a coil of rope over his shoulder, looking down at the merchant boat, which lies in the brown stream with her sail hanging.
Something in the reeds
The river is under mist to the height of a man's chest. The reed tops stand out of it, and from somewhere inside them comes a sound like a bull lowing into an empty cask: three times, then silence.
What is that?
It's a bird, a brown one the size of a hen, and you'll never see it. It makes that noise all spring to find itself a wife.
My mother said it was a drowned ox calling from under the water. My mother was not often right about birds.
Laugh, and pole on slowly
The lookout does the noise back at the reeds, badly, and the reeds answer him. This goes on for some time, and the men are still at it when the mist lifts.
Wait for the sun to burn it off
The sun gets up into it, and the mist goes thin, and then gold, and then it is gone. The reeds are only reeds after all, and the bird, wherever it is, has stopped.

Dawn on a river: white mist lying chest-deep over the water, tall reed heads standing out of it against a pink sky; the boat's mast and the heads and shoulders of three men showing above the mist, all turned toward the reeds.
